confounds: Activity-volume confound: diagnosed users averaged 648.6 retained posts versus 529.8 for controls, so post-level statistics overrepresent diagnosed users relative to their 10.2% user share.

Topic and demographic proxy confound: LGBTQ identity markers occurred in 55.4% of diagnosed users versus 32.6% of controls; fandom/pop-culture language was also more prevalent among diagnosed users, while sports/politics had higher raw post rates among controls. These may reflect community composition, age or collection differences rather than depression.
Explicit mental-health language may encode annotation or recruitment leakage: both labels contain diagnosis, therapy, clinician, advocacy and public-discussion language.
Bereavement, physical illness, relationship conflict, school/work stress and temporary event-related distress can produce overlapping sadness, sleep, death or hopelessness vocabulary.
Near-universal conversational style markers such as mentions, first-person pronouns, quotation marks, laughter and profanity are not clinical evidence and should not be used without semantic context.
Longitudinal repetition may reflect account activity, fandom participation or recurring memes rather than persistent symptoms; source order is not a substitute for observed clinical duration.

caveats: Pronoun and ownership heuristics are imperfect.
A mental-health-focused community or annotation rule may create the association.
Absence of mental-health vocabulary is not evidence for control.
findings.evidence_summary: Mental-specific vocabulary and stronger first-person constructions were consistently more prevalent among diagnosed users across all four development folds.
findings.prompt_guidance: Prioritize owned first-person experience over bare keywords, but require independent symptom or treatment evidence and guard against explicit-diagnosis leakage.

findings.signal: Quotation, third-person, lyric, joke, news, bereavement and physical-illness markers are primarily counterevidence or precision filters, not positive diagnostic signals.

negative_results: Broad appetite/weight, sleep, attention and isolation lexicons were nearly saturated: appetite/weight appeared for 99.5% of diagnosed versus 97.0% of controls, while post-rate ratios were close to 1.0; these terms are too broad alone.

Narrow anhedonia was not stable across folds: diagnosed-minus-control prevalence differences were -0.2, +1.6, +3.9 and +4.4 percentage points across folds 0, 1, 3 and 4. Narrow appetite/weight was also mixed: +7.4, +5.1, -0.3 and +2.8 points.
Broad multi-domain symptom combinations were almost universal (99.2% diagnosed versus 97.6% controls), so domain counting without specificity added little.

Explicit depression vocabulary had substantial false-positive and false-negative potential: it appeared in 25.8% of diagnosed users but also 11.0% of controls, leaving most diagnosed users without such a term.

Context contamination was substantial. Among mental-specific posts, contextual markers such as quotation, music, jokes, news, bereavement or physical-illness framing occurred at similar rates in diagnosed and control users (10.7% versus 10.2%).

Among self-harm/suicide-term posts, joke markers, quotation markers and lyric/music markers were more common in controls than diagnosed users (5.25% versus 2.68%, 4.81% versus 2.23%, and 2.62% versus 1.34%, respectively), supporting aggressive context filtering.

Bereavement and physical-illness vocabulary was not specific: broad bereavement markers had nearly identical post rates in diagnosed and controls (0.754% versus 0.780%), while physical-illness markers were only modestly higher in diagnosed users (0.576% versus 0.505%).
